worked on Rush Street, downstairs, and subsequently at the Blackstone he started to take more active, you know.
And Wayne does, besides the finances, he also books all the bands coming in? Or are you involved in that process?
Well, we both do that.
Ok.

And we get our heads together and we get our heads together and see what’s what, and see who were losses last time and we don’t book them again, or whatever, you know. He takes care of the hotels and all that.
Ok.
And all the banking.
So are you still pretty - you keep pretty current with what these artists are doing today, just to - what their artistic output is?

Oh yeah, yeah. There are a lot of them that I guess we could bring in that would bring a lot of people in, but the music isn’t there. It’s all BS as far as I’m concerned. We have eight million singers who want to come in that can’t sing. They all just holler and scream and all that. And I grew up with big band singers where they stood in one place, they sang, you understood the lyrics, they were in tune, and they work with the band. Now they dance all over the stage, they holler and scream, and blah blah blah. Forget about it.

So do you - just to talk about your taste within the music itself, and just thinking about those particular periods of time where the jazz itself started to go in various directions there. We’re talking about the jazz rock era, and I know there’s some of the musicians that came through that particular period of time that I’ve seen on here through some of the posters. How did that fair within your interest in the music? Was it something that you embraced, or do you find that that integration of the electronic music and jazz rock was something that maybe didn’t have? Because remember, we’re talking volume, I wasn’t sure if I heard you before, volume becomes an issue too. Is that something that you weren’t so crazy about?

Yeah. When a five-piece band is louder than an eighteen-piece big band, something’s wrong as far as I’m concerned. But I even got into the weird stuff with Sun Ra, you know, and he was a trip. He’s funny; he started to believe his own bullshit.
[Laughs] Did he do well when you booked him?
Yeah, yeah. I booked him mostly because of John Gilmore and Pat Patrick on the band.
Ok. I see you also booked the Art Ensemble of Chicago.

Yeah, I dug them. They had some humor about them and some... Lester Bowie has a humor about him. He wasn’t all “oh boy, this is,” you know. And they could play. Don Moye was a marvelous percussionist. And I had heard avant-garde before that; the ACM wasn’t the first ones. Joe Daly and Hal Russell had stuff going way before that. And it was ok, but they came from the straight-ahead stuff, and that’s the kind of avant-garde I like. It was played by people who know how to play straight ahead, because I feel to have freedom, you have to be free from something. You can’t just pick up a horn and go “blblblblbl” which is what a lot of them are doing.

One thing else that I noticed, is that - last night was an example - where there is an acceptance of the audience taking pictures? And you made the comment in advance of course, flash, no flash. But there’s I guess some embracing the fact that this is here and now, we can’t avoid it, so how do we go ahead and embrace it?
Well, Wayne gets mad when I tell them to turn their stuff off, that it’s illegal. I’m very adamant about that. Buy their CDs if you want their music, you know.
Because I saw here maybe half a dozen or less that had their phone out, but they weren’t necessarily taking pictures. They were actually capturing some video elements.
Yeah, I know.
Is there an understanding with them that the act that’s coming in... that that’s something that might?
Well a lot of them don’t say anything. I know in our contract with the - what’s their names - that are coming in...
Yellowjackets?
Yellowjackets. They got it in their contract: Put a sign up, “No recording of any kind.” We will stop playing immediately.
Oh really? Ok.
So that’s what we’ll do. And I’ll announce it. And some people, they don’t know.
Yeah, that’s a tough one there. I mean it’s tough on acts.
Yeah.
It’s just today...
Because everything’s free, you can get it online. I don’t know how the musicians make any money on that.
Yeah, I don’t either. I was just looking at YouTube this morning, just seeing some of the postings on there from the Jazz Showcase, and it goes back to...
Really, we’re on YouTube?
Yeah.
Why? I don’t want it on there.
At the Blackstone I saw the Art Ensemble, 1981, Art Ensemble of Chicago. That’s...
Oh, that was released commercially. That was ok, yeah.
And then there’s a lot more that’s available from here that I’ve saw.
From this venue?
From this venue here, yeah. So it’s, you know... and there’s anywhere from - it looks like a lot of local musicians, some national acts there, but mostly local musicians.
Well some of them when they come in, they get their own people to take videos and they want to... Ow! Oof.
You ok?
Phew! Just gotta stretch it a little.
We’re pretty close to wrapping up here, and then we’ll kind of jump around.
Ok.

So, the last thing - two last things - I want to touch on here: One is - which I find to be very refreshing - when I was just sitting there and watching your audience members coming in, they greeted you, and you greeted them. But there was this - it seemed like a family relationship that you’ve built over many years.
Yeah, yeah. We have a lot of regular people that come in. We used to, when we were at the Blackstone - and on Rush Street - we’d have maybe a hundred or two hundred

people that would always come in regardless of who was playing. They didn’t care, they knew it was good. Except one family from the South Side used to come in just to see Dizzy, and nobody else. So I had to embarrass ‘em one night. I said, “you’re not jazz fans, you’re Dizzy freaks.” So they finally came in to see Yusef one weekend. But yeah, there is a family - because you notice a lot of them are older.
Yeah.
Yeah. So they...

Well there’s one gentleman that - I’m embarrassed I can’t recall his name right now - but he used to play trumpet. He doesn’t play anymore, and he was - we were talking, you came up, and he had some family members, young family members, that were meeting here, and he was helping educate them or bring them into this setting. And I thought, “wow, that’s great!” So they’ve taken on this mission also to make sure the music has an audience and continues to.
Well that’s like I said, I don’t know if you heard it. I said, “then you won’t have to listen to that crap at home.”
Yeah, yeah.
They drive you nuts, drive you out of the house, yeah.

So it was to me - cause I’ve been in some of those places - one particular proprietor was... it was not embracing - this was in New York - it’s like, time, changing sets, get out. Kind of that, and you know, it for me, that’s not what it’s about.
Like the Blue Note?
No, actually...
They don’t tell you to get out, but they just charge you again.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. No I’ve had one of those, in one of the other historic clubs there. But it was unfortunate because of the fact - it’s that you’re building a community; you’re building a base there.
That’s right.
It’s really important that you extend that sense of warmth and greeting and welcoming, and so when you have that it’s like, oh, ok.
That’s true.
It’s challenging. The last bit, the last point I’d like to ask you, is that you are a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master. You’ve been identified as that in a 2015 class there.
Mhmm.

George Coleman is in the class, so is Charles Lloyd, Carla Bley, and you talked about George earlier, so it must be really exciting. What does that mean to you? The nation’s honoring you for something very...

I don’t know. It’s like a lot of people told me, it’s about time and well deserved. I agree with that. The only thing I’m annoyed about is that Down Beat hasn’t written anything about us in years and years. They’re right here in Chicago, and like they say, in your own backyard, you know.
Well hopefully, I know Frank Alkyer is the editor.
Yeah.
Hopefully maybe - maybe this is the...
Maybe this will push it.
Yeah.
Ok.
Yeah, so... Because this is, for me, it’s a true honor to be here, to be able to sit with you and have you tell me your story.
Thank you.
And I will be back many times because this is one of those places to me that really celebrate the music in a big way.
They’re supposed to name some part of the street for me, the city is.
Well let me know when that happens, I’ll come out, and I’ll have a camera, we’ll document that.
Yeah they’ve been so busy with their hitting on each other about the new election coming up for governor and all that, they haven’t paid attention to this, you know. Cause we’re just small fry.
Yeah.
We don’t matter.
With that, we’ll stop this portion of this interview.
Alright.
[Recording fades out]
(Transcribed and edited by Andrew Greene)

segments.title: Opening and introductions
segments.summary: Kimery introduces the interview at the Jazz Showcase in Chicago and asks Segal to start at the beginning.

segments.title: Birth in Philadelphia and his parents
segments.summary: Segal gives his name and birth date, jokes about his mohel, and says his mother Henrietta raised him after his father Irwin left.

segments.title: Big bands at the Earle Theatre and radio
segments.summary: His father takes him to see the big bands at the Earle Theatre, and he hears house bands and Eddie Condon on the radio.

segments.title: Late-night radio remotes and first hearing Bud Powell
segments.summary: He listens secretly to band remotes at night, watches stage shows, and at fifteen hears Bud Powell with Cootie Williams's band at the Pearl Theater.

segments.title: Only child, a failed year of trombone, and his neighborhood
segments.summary: He has no siblings, takes up trombone because his mother vetoed drums, and lives in the Logan section of Philadelphia.

segments.title: Philadelphia radio shows and local young players
segments.summary: He recalls the Horn and Hardart Kiddies Hour, Elliot Lawrence's kid band with Red Rodney, and winning a Woody Herman album on a quiz show.

segments.title: The Downbeat Club and meeting Serge Chaloff
segments.summary: Underage, he gets into Philadelphia's Downbeat Club with Serge Chaloff and hears local musicians such as Specs Wright and Jimmy Heath.

segments.title: Steel Pier in Atlantic City and Ellington's Chelsea Bridge
segments.summary: He describes hearing maturing bands and Ellington at Steel Pier, falling for Chelsea Bridge, and the pier's other attractions.

segments.title: Opera on radio and the Robin Hood Dell
segments.summary: He tells of the Metropolitan Opera broadcasts and Ormandy's Philadelphia Orchestra at the open-air Dell, including the elephant story.

segments.title: The jazz and classical schism, including at Roosevelt
segments.summary: Segal says classical and jazz people were divided, recalling a Roosevelt dean who disliked 'jungle music'.

segments.title: His mother's work, the 1944 draft and discovering Randolph Street
segments.summary: His mother works for the Navy department; he is drafted into the Army Air Corps in 1944 and, stationed in Illinois, discovers Chicago's Randolph Street clubs.

segments.title: Jewish neighborhood, Dobbins Vocational and a missed chance to meet Bechet
segments.summary: He describes his neighborhood and trade school across from Shibe Park, and walking away from a club where Sidney Bechet was playing.

segments.title: Bechet records and his early heroes
segments.summary: He names his first 78 as a Sidney Bechet record, says he never heard Bechet live, and names Red Allen and J.C. Higginbotham as heroes.

segments.title: Downbeat Room on Randolph Street: Red Allen and Red Saunders
segments.summary: On weekend passes he hears Red Allen's band and later Red Saunders with Sonny Cohn at Joe Sherman's Downbeat Room.

segments.title: Boot camp in Texas and Jack Teagarden at the camps
segments.summary: He recalls Texas basic training with a Dixieland band, and hearing Jack Teagarden's band and meeting Billy Byers and Harry Biss.

segments.title: Goofing off in the Army and no famous musicians
segments.summary: He explains his failed radio training, a one-performance try at an entertainment MOS, and that Billy Byers was the most famous musician he met.

segments.title: Favorite trombonists
segments.summary: Asked about trombonists, he praises Teagarden, McGarity, Tizol, Nanton and Bill Harris, and tells of Carl Fontana outblowing a sax section.

segments.title: Weekend passes to Chicago, Elmer's and Jimmy Rainey
segments.summary: He explains his idle Champaign duty, and recalls first hearing jazz at Elmer's with guitarist Jimmy Rainey, plus Jimmy Gourley and Ronny Singer.

segments.title: Settling in Chicago, the Sherman Hotel and the GI Bill at Roosevelt
segments.summary: After discharge he works at the Sherman Hotel, hears the bands, and registers at Roosevelt under the GI Bill around early 1947.

segments.title: Roosevelt courses, boarding with the London family and the Hole
segments.summary: He stays with a Black family on the South Side near the Savoy and Regal, flunks morning classes, and nightly visits the Hole to hear Gene Ammons.

segments.title: Race and neighborhoods in Chicago; Cabrini housing and his marriage
segments.summary: He describes Chicago's racial geography, the jazz center at 63rd and Cottage, living in the mixed Cabrini project, and his Black wife and five children.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Starting the Roosevelt jazz club sessions
segments.summary: He explains how the student jazz club turned into bebop sessions with Ira Sullivan, Richard Davis, Sun Ra's men and a Memphis band including George Coleman.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Seymour's record shop sessions and Sonny Rollins on alto
segments.summary: He turns booking into side work, hosting modern-jazz Saturday sessions at Seymour Schwarz's shop, where Sonny Rollins played alto.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Record store jobs and Half-Price Joe
segments.summary: He worked at Hudson Ross and for Decca distributors, ordering Charlie Parker records, and he started a Parker Christmas album rumor.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: How the Roosevelt sessions were funded
segments.summary: The sessions were volunteer, with a quarter admission rented basses and drums and the money going to the student fund.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Bird's first appearance at Roosevelt and the wire recording
segments.summary: A mix-up over Charlie Ventura's booking leads to Charlie Parker playing the school; a wire recording is made.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Bird at the Bee Hive and the inept sitter-in
segments.summary: After Segal's column about Bird in The Torch, Bird shows up at the Bee Hive and plays until a poor tenor player drives him off.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Last words with Bird in 1953
segments.summary: Segal recounts Bird's last Chicago stand in 1953, his record company question, the narcotics warning, and Ira Sullivan's work with him.

segments.chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
segments.title: Bird's intelligence and the bad Hollywood biopics
segments.summary: Kimery and Segal agree that Parker's brilliance is missed and that the Bird film and The Gene Krupa Story were disgraceful.

segments.title: Becoming a presenter: Gate of Horn, French Poodle and the New York Room
segments.summary: After ten years at Roosevelt he starts presenting weekly jazz at the Gate of Horn, French Poodle and the Sutherland Hotel.

segments.title: Max Roach, Clifford Brown and Red Rodney at the Bee Hive
segments.summary: He recalls a packed Bee Hive for Roach and Brown, a surprise return of Red Rodney, and the groups then on offer.

segments.title: Booking at the North Park Hotel, then Rush Street
segments.summary: He explains how off-night shows grew into weekend bookings of Yusef Lateef, Elvin Jones and Rahsaan Roland Kirk, then moves to Wells and Rush streets.

segments.title: The Jazz Showcase name and the sixties Chicago clubs
segments.summary: He explains the name, lists clubs where he ran off-night sessions, and says musicians were paid whatever was left.

segments.title: Auto plant foreman job and the night Bird's death was announced
segments.summary: He supported himself as a foreman with Wilbur Campbell and others, and recalls Bird's death news interrupting a Roosevelt session in 1955.

segments.title: Charlie Parker memorials and August as Parker month
segments.summary: He tells how Dexter Gordon's departure led to the memorial moving to Bird's August birthday, and who of the bop generation remains.

segments.title: What the Bird celebration plays and what bebop is
segments.summary: He says the month features Bird and bebop tunes, and insists bebop is more than fast notes.

segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie and the 1947 Pershing Ballroom concert
segments.summary: He describes Dizzy as warm and recalls hearing Dizzy's big band with Bird at the Pershing Ballroom.

segments.title: The bent trumpet and Spike Jones's George Rock
segments.summary: He tells of interviewing Spike Jones and seeing trumpeter George Rock with a bent horn before Dizzy announced his.

segments.title: Dizzy at the Jazz Showcase and an evening with Billy Eckstine
segments.summary: He describes Dizzy playing his sessions and North Park shows, and a later meeting with Eckstine.

segments.title: Billy Eckstine's band at the Regal Theater
segments.summary: He recalls Eckstine's band with Miles Davis and Doug Mettome, plus altoist Flap Dungee, in its last week.

segments.title: Dizzy's 1947 band with Chano Pozo on 52nd Street
segments.summary: He saw Dizzy's big band in a tiny 52nd Street room and discusses Afro-Cuban jazz and the street's scene.

segments.title: Dizzy playing the North Park in the sixties
segments.summary: He corrects Kimery's chronology: Dizzy first played for him at the North Park in the sixties.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Johnny Griffin, Joe Henderson and Griffin's drinking
segments.summary: Segal remembers Griffin from Roosevelt, a shared birthday with Joe Henderson, and Griffin's heavy drinking.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Griffin's book, the Hampton band and Roosevelt awards
segments.summary: He recalls what he learned from Griffin's autobiography about the Hampton band, and awards Roosevelt gave.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Lionel Hampton's storm at Grant Park
segments.summary: He tells a story about Hampton playing vibes in a thunderstorm and the lightning hitting the wire.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Wayne takes over the business side; hotels and four-night runs
segments.summary: He says Wayne handles licenses and money, and explains the cost of rooms and why multi-night runs beat one-nighters.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Clubs versus concerts, local artists and university ties
segments.summary: They discuss club residencies, local players weekdays, and ties with Roosevelt, Columbia and DePaul.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Sunday matinees
segments.summary: He explains the matinees started at the French Poodle, draw families and older people, and sometimes include explanations.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: A hangout where musicians get in free
segments.summary: He says musicians drop in free, recalling Roosevelt fake musicians with closed cases, and wanting a hangout like the Green Mill.

segments.chapter: Johnny Griffin, Hampton and club life
segments.title: Why musicians need to hear each other, and whether today's drummers swing
segments.summary: They discuss live learning, swing, and how drummers like Roach, Blakey and Roy Haynes accompanied rather than overpowered.

segments.title: Great drummers Segal heard
segments.summary: He lists drummers who played for him, including Sid Catlett, Bellson, Philly Joe Jones, and Dave Tough, and discusses Stan Levey.

segments.title: The Basie band with Nat Pierce and Joe Williams
segments.summary: He recalls booking the Basie band while Basie was ill, when Joe Williams sat in.

segments.title: Thad Jones and Mel Lewis band; Duffy Jackson in Florida
segments.summary: They sort out who was drumming in Basie's band, and he tells of a Florida stand with Thad Jones leading.

segments.title: Chubby Jackson, his kids' TV show and Chubby's Back
segments.summary: He talks about Chubby Jackson, his Chicago children's TV show and big band for Chess.

segments.title: Joe's Bebop Cafe on Navy Pier and the Grand Avenue club
segments.summary: He tells how the Showcase got a Navy Pier spot, Joe's Bebop Cafe, plus Clark and Grand.

segments.title: Navy Pier nightly bands and finding the Grand Avenue space
segments.summary: After a break he describes Navy Pier's nightly music, losing the leases and the Grand Avenue club.

segments.title: Live recordings from the club
segments.summary: Few recordings from the Showcase came out; the unreleased tapes will go to the Roosevelt archives.

segments.title: Chess reissues and Moody's Flute 'N The Blues
segments.summary: He edited Chess reissues in the sixties and produced James Moody's Flute 'N The Blues.

segments.title: James Moody and the Star Spangled Banner
segments.summary: He recalls befriending Moody and Moody's North Park routine with Gene Ammons.

segments.title: Finding and building the Dearborn Station space
segments.summary: He and Wayne chose a space in Dearborn Station and remodeled it from scratch.

segments.title: Financing the club and Wayne as the main man
segments.summary: He leaves the loan negotiations to Wayne, who took over around the Grand Avenue years.

segments.title: Wife Helen and his children
segments.summary: He names his wife Helen and his five children, only Wayne in music.

segments.title: Wayne's path into the business and booking together
segments.summary: Wayne went from disco to working with him at the North Park, Rush Street and the Blackstone, and now they book together.

segments.title: Today's singers and bookings
segments.summary: He complains that modern singers shout rather than sing, unlike the big band singers he grew up with.

segments.title: Jazz rock, volume and booking Sun Ra
segments.summary: He dislikes loud small bands but booked Sun Ra for Gilmore and Patrick.

segments.title: Art Ensemble of Chicago and avant-garde
segments.summary: He praises the Art Ensemble and says avant-garde works when players can play straight ahead.

segments.title: Phones, taping and 'no recording' contracts
segments.summary: He enforces no recording, and the Yellowjackets contract has a clause.

segments.title: Online music and club videos
segments.summary: Segal wonders how musicians earn money with free music and is surprised the club is on YouTube.

segments.title: The Showcase regulars as family
segments.summary: They discuss regular older audiences, Dizzy freaks and welcoming audiences compared with New York clubs.

segments.title: Being named an NEA Jazz Master
segments.summary: He reacts to the 2015 NEA Jazz Master honor and is annoyed Down Beat ignores the club.

segments.title: Closing thanks and a street naming
segments.summary: Kimery thanks Segal, mentions a street naming, and ends the session.
